items.title: Classifying Bodies — Constitutional vs Statutory vs Executive
items.body:
**In one line**
Every public body in India belongs to one of three families, and the family it belongs to depends only on *who created it* — the Constitution, a law, or a government order.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC and UPSC love to test whether you can slot a body (NITI Aayog, NHRC, Election Commission) into the right family, because candidates routinely mix them up.

**The story**
When India needed new institutions over the decades, it created them in three different ways, and that choice decides how strong and how permanent the body is.

| Type | Created by | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Constitutional** | Named in the Constitution itself | Election Commission (Art 324), CAG (Art 148), UPSC (Art 315), Finance Commission (Art 280) |
| **Statutory** | An ordinary Act of Parliament or a State Legislature | NHRC, CVC, SEBI, NGT, Lokpal, NCW, NCM, CIC, NDMA, UGC |
| **Executive (non-statutory)** | A simple government resolution or order | NITI Aayog, Law Commission of India |

A constitutional body is the hardest to touch — changing it needs a constitutional amendment. A statutory body can be changed by passing or editing an ordinary law. An executive body can be created or dissolved overnight by the government.

Non-constitutional bodies exist because they give the state **flexibility** (create or wind up without amending the Constitution), supply **sectoral expertise** (finance, environment, human rights), and handle **policy implementation and regulation**. The Planning Commission (1950) was the earliest major one; it was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.

**Terms explained**
- **Constitutional body** — a body whose existence is written into the Constitution.
- **Statutory body** — a body set up by an Act (a law) passed by a legislature.
- **Executive / non-statutory body** — a body set up by a government decision, with no special law behind it.

**Don't confuse**
- **NITI Aayog is NOT statutory** — it was created by a 2015 executive resolution, so it is an executive body (a very common trap).
- **Finance Commission (constitutional) vs NITI Aayog (executive)** — both deal with money/planning, but their source of authority is completely different.

**Remember it**
Source test: in the Constitution = constitutional; in an Act = statutory; in a resolution = executive.

**TL;DR**
- Constitutional = named in the Constitution (ECI, CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission).
- Statutory = created by an Act (NHRC, CVC, SEBI, NGT, Lokpal, CIC).
- Executive = created by a resolution (NITI Aayog, Law Commission).
- NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015 and cannot allocate funds.
keyPoints: Constitutional bodies are named in the Constitution (ECI, CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission).
Statutory bodies are created by an Act of Parliament (NHRC, CVC, SEBI, NGT, Lokpal, CIC).
Executive/non-statutory bodies are created by a government resolution (NITI Aayog, Law Commission).
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015 and has no fund-allocation power.
Non-constitutional bodies offer flexibility, sectoral expertise and policy-implementation roles.
items.mnemonic: Source test: in the Constitution = constitutional; in an Act = statutory; in a resolution = executive.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Non-Constitutional Bodies (Background, History, Importance)

items.title: Anti-Corruption & Investigative Watchdogs — CBI, CVC, Lokpal
items.body:
**In one line**
Three bodies police corruption in India — the CBI investigates, the CVC supervises and advises, and the Lokpal inquires into the top public functionaries.

**Why it is asked**
Their founding laws, years and powers are classic one-mark facts, and the exam often mixes up which body does what.

**The story**
India built its anti-corruption machinery in layers over time.

- **CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation)** — traces to the **Special Police Establishment (1941)**, set up to tackle wartime supply corruption; reconstituted as the CBI in **1963**. Its legal power comes from the **Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946**, and it works under the **Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions**. It needs a **State's general consent** to operate in that State (and the State can withdraw it). It is headed by a Director with a minimum 2-year tenure.
- **CVC (Central Vigilance Commission)** — set up in **1964** on the **Santhanam Committee's** recommendation; became **statutory under the CVC Act, 2003**. It is a multi-member body: a **Central Vigilance Commissioner plus two Vigilance Commissioners**, appointed by the President. It can **direct the CBI** to investigate and supervises Chief Vigilance Officers.
- **Lokpal & Lokayuktas** — created by the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**: a Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in the States. Composition: **1 Chairperson + up to 8 members**, at least **half of them judicial**. It inquires into corruption allegations against public functionaries, including ministers. India's first Lokpal Chairperson was **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (2019)**. Andhra Pradesh had a Lokayukta earlier, under the **AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983**.

**Terms explained**
- **General consent** — a standing permission from a State that lets the CBI investigate there without asking case by case.
- **Statutory status** — being backed by a specific Act, which makes a body harder to abolish than a mere order.
- **Judicial member** — a member who has been a judge, giving the body legal expertise.

**Don't confuse**
- **CBI (investigates) vs CVC (supervises/advises) vs Lokpal (inquires at the top)** — three different roles.
- **CVC became statutory only in 2003**, although it was set up in 1964.

**Remember it**
CBI investigates, CVC advises/directs, Lokpal inquires into corruption at the top.

**TL;DR**
- CBI: SPE 1941 → CBI 1963; DSPE Act 1946; under Ministry of Personnel; needs State consent.
- CVC: 1964 (Santhanam Committee); statutory 2003; CVC + 2 Vigilance Commissioners; can direct the CBI.
- Lokpal: 2013 Act; 1 Chairperson + up to 8 members, half judicial; first Chair Justice P.C. Ghose (2019).
- AP's Lokayukta dates to the AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983.
keyPoints: CBI: SPE 1941 → CBI 1963; DSPE Act 1946; under Ministry of Personnel; needs State consent.
CVC: 1964 (Santhanam Committee); statutory 2003; CVC + 2 Vigilance Commissioners; can direct CBI.
Lokpal: 2013 Act; 1 Chairperson + up to 8 members, half judicial; probes ministers/officials.
First Lokpal Chairperson was Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (2019).
AP established its Lokayukta under the AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983.
items.mnemonic: CBI investigates, CVC advises/directs, Lokpal prosecutes corruption at the top.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Non-Constitutional Bodies (CBI, CVC, Lokpal); AP Lokayukta Act 1983

items.title: Rights & Welfare Commissions — NHRC, SHRC, NCW, NCM
items.body:
**In one line**
Four statutory commissions protect rights in India — the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions for human rights, and the NCW and NCM for women and minorities.

**Why it is asked**
The 2019 NHRC amendment, the armed-forces limitation and the "recommendatory only" nature are frequently tested, and candidates confuse these with the constitutional SC/ST commissions.

**The story**
- **NHRC and SHRCs** — both are created under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**. After the **2019 amendment**, the NHRC **Chairperson** can be a person who has been **Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court** (earlier only a retired CJI), and the term was cut from 5 years to **3 years**. The NHRC has **recommendatory powers only** and **cannot directly investigate the armed forces** — it asks the Central government for a report. **State Human Rights Commissions**, under the same 1993 Act, inquire into violations relatable to **State List and Concurrent List** subjects of the Seventh Schedule.
- **NCW and NCM** — the **National Commission for Women (1992)** and the **National Commission for Minorities (1992)** are **statutory, advisory** bodies. They review safeguards, investigate grievances and recommend reforms, but **cannot enforce** their recommendations.

Keep these separate from the **constitutional** commissions for SCs (Art 338), STs (Art 338A) and Backward Classes (Art 338B) — those are written into the Constitution, not created by an ordinary statute.

**Terms explained**
- **Recommendatory power** — the body can only advise or suggest; the government is not legally bound to obey.
- **State List / Concurrent List** — two of the three lists in the Seventh Schedule that divide subjects between the Centre and the States; the Concurrent List is shared by both.

**Don't confuse**
- **NHRC/NCW/NCM = statutory**, but **SC/ST/BC commissions (Art 338 series) = constitutional**.
- **NHRC cannot itself probe the armed forces** — it only seeks a report; do not tick an option that says it investigates them directly.

**Remember it**
Commissions for SC/ST/BC = constitutional (338 series); Women/Minorities/Human Rights = statutory.

**TL;DR**
- NHRC and SHRCs: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
- 2019 amendment: Chairperson can be CJI or an SC judge; term 5 → 3 years.
- NHRC is recommendatory and cannot directly investigate the armed forces.
- NCW (1992) and NCM (1992) are statutory advisory bodies with no enforcement power.
keyPoints: NHRC and SHRCs are created under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
2019 amendment: Chairperson can be CJI or an SC judge; term cut from 5 to 3 years.
NHRC is recommendatory and cannot directly investigate the armed forces.
SHRCs cover human-rights violations on State List and Concurrent List subjects.
NCW (1992) and NCM (1992) are statutory advisory bodies with no enforcement power.
items.mnemonic: Commissions for SC/ST/BC = constitutional (338 series); Women/Minorities/Human Rights = statutory.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Non-Constitutional Bodies (NHRC, NCW, NCM); Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act 2019

items.title: Sectoral Regulators — SEBI, RBI, TRAI, IRDAI, PFRDA, CCI
items.body:
**In one line**
Sectoral regulators are statutory bodies that run one slice of the economy — banking, markets, telecom, insurance, pensions or competition — by making rules, supervising and punishing violators.

**Why it is asked**
Matching each regulator to its Act and year is a staple one-mark question, and the "constitutional vs statutory" trap recurs for the RBI and SEBI.

**The story**
As the economy opened up, India created specialised regulators so that experts, not generalist ministries, could govern technical sectors.

| Regulator | Sector | Statutory basis |
|---|---|---|
| **RBI** | Banking, monetary policy | RBI Act, 1934 (began 1935) |
| **SEBI** | Securities / capital market | Set up 1988; SEBI Act, 1992 |
| **IRDAI** | Insurance | IRDA Act, 1999 |
| **PFRDA** | Pensions (NPS) | PFRDA Act, 2013 |
| **TRAI** | Telecom | TRAI Act, 1997 |
| **CCI** | Competition / anti-trust | Competition Act, 2002 (operational 2009) |

Each regulator combines three jobs: **rule-making** (legislative), **supervision** (executive) and **adjudication** (quasi-judicial). They can frame regulations, investigate and impose penalties. The **CCI** replaced the older MRTP regime (MRTP Act, 1969) and now checks anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance and large mergers. None of these bodies is named in the Constitution — all are statutory.

**Terms explained**
- **Regulator** — a body that writes and enforces the rules of one sector.
- **Quasi-judicial** — court-like power to hear disputes and impose penalties, without being a full court.
- **Abuse of dominance** — a powerful firm using its market strength unfairly, which the CCI can act against.

**Don't confuse**
- **RBI and SEBI are statutory, NOT constitutional** — a very common trap.
- **SEBI's year** — it was *set up* in 1988 but became *statutory* only with the SEBI Act, 1992.
- **CCI (Competition Act 2002) replaced the MRTP Act, 1969** — do not treat MRTP as the body-creating law for the CCI.

**Remember it**
Regulator years: RBI '34, SEBI '92, TRAI '97, IRDAI '99, CCI '02, PFRDA '13.

**TL;DR**
- RBI: RBI Act, 1934 (began 1935); SEBI: set up 1988, statutory 1992.
- TRAI (1997), IRDAI (1999), PFRDA (2013) regulate telecom, insurance, pensions.
- CCI: Competition Act, 2002 (operational 2009); replaced the MRTP regime.
- Regulators mix rule-making, supervision and quasi-judicial penalty powers.
keyPoints: RBI: statutory under the RBI Act, 1934; began operations in 1935.
SEBI: set up 1988, statutory under the SEBI Act, 1992.
TRAI (1997), IRDAI (1999) and PFRDA (2013) regulate telecom, insurance and pensions.
CCI: Competition Act, 2002 (operational 2009); replaced the MRTP regime.
Regulators combine rule-making, supervision and quasi-judicial penalty powers.
items.mnemonic: Regulator years: RBI '34, SEBI '92, TRAI '97, IRDAI '99, CCI '02, PFRDA '13.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Non-Constitutional Bodies (SEBI, CCI); RBI/TRAI/IRDA/PFRDA Acts

items.title: Quasi-Judicial Bodies & Tribunals — NGT, CAT, Art 323A/323B
items.body:
**In one line**
Tribunals are specialised, court-like bodies that deliver quick expert justice in areas such as service disputes and the environment, and the Constitution expressly provides for them.

**Why it is asked**
Articles 323A/323B, the NGT's binding orders and the recent 2025 Supreme Court verdict on tribunal independence are high-value current-affairs plus static facts.

**The story**
To ease the burden on regular courts and bring in specialists, India created tribunals.

- The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added **Article 323A** (administrative tribunals, such as the **Central Administrative Tribunal** for service matters) and **Article 323B** (tribunals for taxation, environment and similar subjects).
- The **National Green Tribunal (NGT)** was created under the **NGT Act, 2010**. It is a **quasi-judicial** body for environmental disputes, with a bench of **judicial members plus expert (scientific) members**, headed by a retired Supreme Court judge (or an eligible High Court Chief Justice). Its orders are **binding**, it can award compensation, and appeals lie to the **Supreme Court**.
- The **Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021** rationalised several tribunals and set members' service conditions. In **November 2025 the Supreme Court struck down key provisions**, holding that excessive executive control over appointments, tenure and funding **violated judicial independence and the separation of powers**, and directed the Centre to set up a **National Tribunal Commission**.

**Terms explained**
- **Tribunal** — a specialised body that decides disputes in one field faster and more cheaply than ordinary courts.
- **Quasi-judicial** — having court-like decision-making power without being a formal court.
- **Separation of powers** — the principle that the legislature, executive and judiciary stay independent of one another.

**Don't confuse**
- **323A (Administrative tribunals) vs 323B (other/Broader subjects)** — do not swap them.
- The **NGT is headed by a retired Supreme Court judge, not a serving Chief Justice of India**.

**Remember it**
323A = Administrative tribunals; 323B = other (Broader) subjects.

**TL;DR**
- 42nd Amendment (1976) added Articles 323A (administrative/CAT) and 323B (other tribunals).
- NGT (NGT Act, 2010): quasi-judicial, judicial + expert members, binding orders.
- Appeals against NGT orders lie to the Supreme Court.
- November 2025: the Supreme Court struck down key parts of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
keyPoints: 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 323A (administrative tribunals/CAT) and 323B (other tribunals).
NGT (NGT Act, 2010) is quasi-judicial with judicial + expert members; orders are binding.
Appeals against NGT orders lie to the Supreme Court.
Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 rationalised tribunals and altered service conditions.
In November 2025 the Supreme Court struck down key provisions for undermining tribunal independence.
items.source: Constitution Arts 323A/323B; NGT Act 2010; Supreme Court Tribunals Reforms judgment (2025)

items.title: Transparency & Other Statutory Bodies — CIC, Law Commission, NDMA, UGC, FTII
items.body:
**In one line**
A set of statutory and executive bodies handles transparency (CIC), legal reform (Law Commission), disaster management (NDMA) and education (UGC, FTII).

**Why it is asked**
The 2019 RTI amendment, the Law Commission's non-statutory status and "who chairs the NDMA" are repeat questions.

**The story**
- **CIC (Central Information Commission)** — set up under the **Right to Information Act, 2005** to secure citizens' access to information. It has a **Chief Information Commissioner plus up to 10 Information Commissioners**, can order disclosure and impose penalties. The **RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** let the Centre prescribe the **tenure and salaries** of Commissioners (earlier a fixed 5-year term) — criticised as diluting its independence.
- Other important bodies:

| Body | Basis | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Law Commission** | Government resolution (1955) | **Non-statutory**, advisory legal-reform body |
| **NDMA** | Disaster Management Act, 2005 | Statutory; **PM is ex-officio Chairperson** |
| **UGC** | UGC Act, 1956 | Statutory; regulates higher education and funding |
| **FTII** | Established 1960 | Statutory institute for film and TV education |

The **Law Commission** only recommends reforms; its advice is **not binding**. At the State level, the **Chief Minister** chairs the State Disaster Management Authority.

**Terms explained**
- **Ex-officio** — holding a post automatically because of another office (the PM chairs the NDMA simply by being PM).
- **Non-statutory body** — one with no backing Act, set up by a government order.

**Don't confuse**
- **Law Commission = non-statutory**, even though it recommends laws.
- **NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister**, not the Home Minister.
- **CIC was created by the RTI Act 2005**, but it was the **2019 amendment** that changed tenure/salary powers.

**Remember it**
RTI 2005 built the CIC; the RTI 2019 amendment trimmed its independence.

**TL;DR**
- CIC: created under the RTI Act, 2005; CIC + up to 10 Information Commissioners.
- RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 let the Centre fix Commissioners' tenure and salaries.
- Law Commission (1955) is a non-statutory advisory body; its advice is not binding.
- NDMA (Disaster Management Act, 2005) is chaired ex-officio by the PM; UGC (1956) and FTII (1960) are statutory.
keyPoints: CIC created under the RTI Act, 2005; CIC + up to 10 Information Commissioners.
RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 let the Centre fix Commissioners' tenure and salaries.
Law Commission of India (1955) is a non-statutory advisory body; advice not binding.
NDMA (Disaster Management Act, 2005) is chaired ex-officio by the Prime Minister.
UGC (UGC Act, 1956) regulates higher education; FTII (1960) trains for film & TV.
items.mnemonic: RTI 2005 built the CIC; RTI 2019 amendment trimmed its independence.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Non-Constitutional Bodies (CIC, Law Commission, NDMA, UGC, FTII); RTI Act 2005 & 2019

items.title: PYQ Precision — NALSA, Gram Nyayalayas & Commodity Boards
items.body:
**In one line**
A cluster of bodies delivers justice at the grassroots (NALSA, Gram Nyayalayas) and regulates commodities (Tea Board), and each carries one precise fact the exam loves to flip.

**Why it is asked**
These are direct UPSC/APPSC previous-year questions where a single wrong detail (ministry, headquarters, civil-only) decides the answer.

**The story**
- **Access-to-justice bodies**:

| Body | Statute | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| **NALSA** | Legal Services Authorities Act **1987** | Free legal aid to weaker sections; patron-in-chief = **CJI**; runs **Lok Adalats**; guides State Legal Services Authorities |
| **Gram Nyayalayas** | Gram Nyayalayas Act **2008** (operational 2009) | Mobile village courts; try **both civil AND criminal** cases; allow **social activists as mediators**; headed by a **Nyayadhikari** |

- **Commodity Boards** (statutory, under the Ministry of Commerce & Industry): the **Tea Board** is statutory, works under the **Ministry of Commerce** (NOT Agriculture), has its **headquarters at Kolkata**, and keeps overseas offices (Dubai, Moscow). The Coffee, Rubber, Spices and Tobacco Boards are likewise statutory under the Ministry of Commerce.
- **Forest Rights Act 2006** — administered by the **Ministry of Tribal Affairs**; it recognises individual and community forest rights, and the **Gram Sabha** initiates the claim process.

**Terms explained**
- **Lok Adalat** — a "people's court" that settles disputes by compromise; its award is binding.
- **Nyayadhikari** — the presiding officer of a Gram Nyayalaya, of the rank of a Judicial Magistrate First Class.
- **Gram Sabha** — the assembly of all adult voters of a village.

**Don't confuse**
- **Gram Nyayalayas try BOTH civil and criminal cases** — not civil-only.
- **Tea Board: Ministry of Commerce (not Agriculture), HQ Kolkata (not Bengaluru)**.
- **Forest Rights Act nodal ministry = Tribal Affairs**, not Environment.

**Remember it**
One fact flips each answer: Gram Nyayalayas = civil + criminal; Tea Board = Commerce + Kolkata; FRA = Tribal Affairs.

**TL;DR**
- NALSA: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; patron-in-chief CJI; runs Lok Adalats.
- Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008: mobile village courts, both civil and criminal, activists as mediators.
- Tea Board: statutory, Ministry of Commerce, HQ Kolkata.
- Forest Rights Act 2006 nodal ministry = Ministry of Tribal Affairs; Gram Sabha initiates claims.
keyPoints: NALSA — Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; patron-in-chief CJI; free legal aid; runs Lok Adalats; guides State authorities.
Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008 — mobile village courts try BOTH civil and criminal cases; permit social activists as mediators.
Tea Board is statutory, under the Ministry of Commerce (not Agriculture), HQ Kolkata (not Bengaluru).
Commodity Boards (Tea/Coffee/Rubber/Spices/Tobacco) are statutory under the Ministry of Commerce.
Forest Rights Act 2006 nodal ministry = Ministry of Tribal Affairs; Gram Sabha initiates claims.
items.source: UPSC 2013/2016/2019/2021 Prelims (Rau's IAS COMPASS); Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008

items.title: For Mains — Statutory, Regulatory & Quasi-Judicial Bodies
items.body:
Mains (GS-3, clause M3-9) does not ask you to name founding years; it asks you to **evaluate** whether India's non-constitutional bodies are independent, effective and accountable. Frame answers around the dimensions below.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Rationale** | Flexibility (no amendment needed), sectoral expertise, speedy specialised justice, relief to overburdened courts |
| **Functions** | Regulators fuse legislative (rule-making) + executive (supervision) + judicial (adjudication) roles; watchdogs probe corruption; commissions protect rights |
| **Significance** | Investor/consumer confidence (SEBI, CCI), environmental protection (NGT), human-rights redress (NHRC), transparency (CIC) |
| **Criticism / limitations** | Fragile independence in appointments, tenure, funding; government is the largest litigant before tribunals it also staffs; regulatory capture; vacancies and delays; mostly recommendatory (NHRC, NCW) |
| **Way forward** | Independent selection committees, secure tenure, financial autonomy, a National Tribunal Commission, performance review |

**Data points / authorities to quote**
- **Supreme Court, November 2025** — struck down key provisions of the **Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021** and ordered a **National Tribunal Commission** (judicial independence, separation of powers).
- **RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** — let the Centre fix CIC tenure/salaries, criticised as diluting independence.
- **Madras Bar Association** line of judgments on tribunal independence; **2nd ARC** on regulatory governance.
- **99th Amendment / NJAC (2015)** struck down — the courts guarding institutional independence.
- **NHRC** (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993) — recommendatory, cannot probe armed forces directly.

**AP angle**
The **AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983** shows States pioneering anti-corruption bodies before the 2013 central law; AP's State Information Commission and SHRC illustrate cooperative implementation.

**Use in answers**
- *Example*: cite the 2025 tribunals verdict to show the judiciary defending independence.
- *Quote*: "Justice must not only be done but independent to be seen as done."
- *Diagram idea*: a triangle — Rule-making, Supervision, Adjudication — with "independence in appointments/tenure/funding" as the base holding it up.
keyPoints: Evaluate on rationale, functions, significance, criticism and way forward (not static years).
Regulators fuse legislative, executive and quasi-judicial roles; this raises separation-of-powers concerns.
Core critique: fragile independence in appointments, tenure and funding; government is largest litigant.
Quote the November 2025 SC verdict on the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 and the National Tribunal Commission.
RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and the NJAC (2015) illustrate threats to and defence of institutional independence.
AP angle: Lokayukta under the AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983.
items.source: Constitution Arts 323A/323B; SC Tribunals Reforms judgment (Nov 2025); RTI Act 2005 & 2019; 2nd ARC
